title: 251. Functions, Graphs & Transformations: Distinguishing Discrete and Continuous Domains
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Distinguishing Discrete and Continuous Domains from a Set
questions.learningObjective: Identify a discrete domain from a given set of input values.
questions.question: Which of the following describes a discrete domain?
questions.explanation: A discrete domain consists of separate, isolated input values. The set \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) contains only the four distinct numbers \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), so it is discrete. The interval of all real numbers between \(1\) and \(4\) is continuous because it contains every real number in that range. Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: A discrete domain contains separate values rather than an unbroken interval.

questions.concept: Discrete Domain from a Finite List of Inputs
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a finite list of input values gives a discrete domain.
questions.question: A function is defined only at \(x=1\), \(x=2\), and \(x=3\). Is its domain discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: The function is defined only at the three separate input values \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\). There is no unbroken interval of input values, so the domain is discrete. Therefore option A is correct.
questions.hint: Check whether the allowed inputs form separate values or an unbroken interval.

questions.concept: Discrete Domain in a Counting Context
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a counting context produces a discrete domain.
questions.question: The number of books on shelf \(n\) is recorded for shelf numbers \(1,2,3,\ldots\). Is the domain of shelf numbers discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: Shelf numbers are separate counting values such as \(1,2,3,\ldots\). They do not form an unbroken interval of real numbers. Therefore the domain of shelf numbers is discrete, so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Counting values are usually separate rather than forming an interval.

questions.concept: Continuous Domain in a Time Interval
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a real time interval gives a continuous domain.
questions.question: A temperature is recorded continuously over the time interval \(0\le t\le 10\) hours. Is the domain of times discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: The time interval \(0\le t\le 10\) contains every real number between \(0\) and \(10\), not just separate counting values. Therefore the domain of times is continuous, so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Decide whether the recorded times include every real value between the endpoints or only separate values.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain type when a graph consists of separate unconnected points.
questions.question: A graph consists of separate unconnected points. Is its domain discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: A graph made of separate unconnected points has input values that are isolated from one another. There is no unbroken interval of inputs. Therefore its domain is discrete, so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Look at whether the graph covers an unbroken interval of \(x\)-values.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a domain given by an inequality is continuous.
questions.question: A function has domain \(0\le x\le 1\). Is this domain discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: The inequality \(0\le x\le 1\) includes every real number between \(0\) and \(1\), not only separate values. Therefore the domain is continuous, so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Decide which real numbers satisfy the inequality and whether any gaps are left between them.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether the set of natural numbers gives a discrete domain.
questions.question: A function is defined only for natural numbers \(x=1,2,3,\ldots\). Is its domain discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: The natural numbers \(1,2,3,\ldots\) are separate counting values with gaps between them. They do not form an unbroken interval of real numbers. Therefore the domain is discrete, so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Counting numbers are separate values rather than all real numbers in an interval.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a table of selected input values gives a discrete domain.
questions.question: A function is given by a table with \(x\)-values \(0\), \(1\), \(2\), \(3\). Is its domain discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: The table lists only the separate input values \(0\), \(1\), \(2\), \(3\). It does not define the function for every real number in an interval. Therefore the domain is discrete, so option A is correct.
questions.hint: A table usually lists selected input values rather than every value in an interval.

questions.concept: Continuous Domain from a Smooth Curve
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a smooth unbroken curve has a continuous domain.
questions.question: A graph is a smooth curve with no breaks from \(x=-2\) to \(x=2\). Is its domain discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: The graph covers every \(x\)-value from \(-2\) to \(2\) without breaks. Therefore its domain is the interval \([-2,2]\), which is continuous. Hence option A is correct.
questions.hint: An unbroken graph over an interval indicates that every value in the interval is included.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether daily measurements produce a discrete domain.
questions.question: The height of a plant is measured once each day for \(30\) days. Is the domain of measurement times discrete or continuous?
questions.explanation: The measurements are taken only once each day, so the times form the separate values day \(1\), day \(2\), and so on up to day \(30\). These are isolated points, not every real time in the \(30\)-day interval. Therefore the domain of measurement times is discrete, so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Consider whether measurements are taken at every possible time or only at separate selected times.
